strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP need: compact generative models for ten Indian languages, including underserved languages such as Assamese, Odia, Konkani, Maithili, and Sanskrit.

The reported 13.29–367.5M parameter models, single-GPU training, and CPU inference target practically valuable resource constraints. Language-specific corpus curation and culturally grounded instructions are worthwhile contributions to pursue.

The inclusion of native-speaker judgments, explicit prompts, and extensive generated examples enables qualitative scrutiny. Evaluating grammar, coherence, creativity, and factuality recognizes distinct aspects of generation quality.
weaknesses: Essential methodology is missing, preventing reproduction and assessment of the claimed technical novelty. The novel architecture is not specified, Section 4.4 on tokenization is empty, and model configurations, vocabulary construction, training hyperparameters, corpus sizes, and precise data provenance are absent. The stated 95/5 split does not explain split granularity or overlap prevention. Promised future API access does not resolve these omissions.

Result attribution contains substantive inconsistencies. Table 5 attributes Bangla generations to the 87.25M model, while Table 12 attributes the same continuations to the 108.5M model, despite different reported ratings for these models. Several Sanskrit outputs attributed to GPT-Neo/GPT2-XL in Table 20 reappear under BLOOM labels in Table 21, which also contains mismatched prompt prefixes. Original generation logs and annotations need auditing before the comparative scores can be trusted.

The human evaluation is too small and insufficiently documented for the central claims: four prompts per language for only Bangla, Hindi, and Sanskrit, nominally with three generations each. Evaluator allocation, detailed rating guidelines, blinding, agreement, and uncertainty are unspecified. Table 5 inconsistently refers to three versus five generations. Assigning factuality zero when a claim cannot be verified conflates uncertainty with falsehood. Instruction-following capabilities are supported by screenshots without systematic held-out evaluation.

The comparisons do not establish broad superiority over capable Indic models. Many baselines are predominantly English models, and relevant Indic-focused baselines are missing. ChatGPT is evaluated through website conversations using text fragments, without a reproducible protocol controlling conversation history, task instructions, model version, and decoding. These results cannot establish that the competing systems generally cannot generate coherent text in the target languages.

The proposed explanations for performance are not experimentally isolated. There are no controlled comparisons separating architecture, tokenizer, corpus quality, language balancing, and script grouping. Differences between BLOOM model sizes with fixed language coverage do not demonstrate the curse of multilinguality. Likewise, tokenizing an unseen language written in a familiar script does not establish generation competence in that language.

Table 2 provides perplexities without adequately characterized evaluation corpora or matched baselines. In particular, per-token perplexity across the two Konkani–Maithili tokenizers is not directly comparable without a common normalization, such as bits per byte. Consequently, these numbers do not substantiate tokenizer superiority or broad model quality.

The efficiency claims exceed the measurements. Section 6 infers a 20–66-fold speedup from parameter-count ratios, which is not a valid latency comparison. Table 11 omits CPU hardware, threading, inference implementation, workload details, and measured baseline speeds; training duration and total compute are also missing. Establishing a publishable contribution requires substantial methods documentation, an audit of reported results, and new controlled evaluations. These soundness and reproducibility gaps motivate resubmission after next cycle.
